title: A Tale of Two Markets: A Dickensian Take on the Coming Years in Defense Tech
gist: Ben FitzGerald argues defense tech has split into two markets: a small 'London' of production-contract startups (Palantir, Anduril, Saronic) priced at extreme revenue multiples, and a chaotic 'Paris' of prototype-dependent startups living on discretionary RDT&E money. With early-2020s venture funds fully deployed and only 14% of DIU prototype OTAs converting to production, he expects quiet capital exhaustion, distressed M&A and roll-ups, and says production-contract awards are the only leading indicator worth watching.

insights.claim: Defense technology has split into two distinct markets: a production market of programs of record and recurring revenue, and a prototype market of pilots and discretionary funding, and each must be assessed separately.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Investors should segment defense-tech exposure by production vs prototype revenue rather than treating the sector as one trade.
insights.quote: Defense technology has evolved into two distinct markets.
insights.locator: Defense technology has evolved into two

insights.claim: Headline signals of record capital, valuations and budgets coexist with growing unease among defense-tech investors because production contracts remain elusive and many startups cannot extend runway across the valley of death.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Sector headlines overstate breadth of health; dispersion between winners and losers is the real story.
insights.quote: Production contracts remain as elusive as ever, and a generation of startups is struggling to extend their runways across the valley of death
insights.locator: It's a strange time for the

insights.claim: Reported annual recurring revenue at prototype-heavy defense startups is often cobbled-together RDT&E, pilot and innovation funds that are vulnerable to sweeps, reallocation to current operations, and continuing-resolution bans on new starts.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Diligence on defense startups should discount 'ARR' that is actually discretionary funding.
insights.quote: What is presented to boards as annual recurring revenue is often cobbled together research, development, test and evaluation dollars, pilot budgets, and innovation funding

themes.theme: Scale mismatch: capital vs contract flow

insights.claim: Around $49 billion of venture investment went to defense technology in 2025, and the Silicon Valley Defense Group's top 100 startups have raised over $118 billion in total.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Capital deployed vastly exceeds contract revenue, setting up a return-generation problem.
insights.quote: Around $49 billion in venture investment was allocated to defense technology in 2025.
insights.locator: It is the Best of Times

insights.claim: Palantir is valued at over $400 billion, more than Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman and General Dynamics combined.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Valuation gap between new entrants and primes reflects growth expectations that program delays can puncture.
insights.quote: Palantir is now valued at over $400 billion, greater than Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, and General Dynamics combined.
insights.locator: It is the Best of Times

insights.claim: The Defense Department obligates over $450 billion annually in contracts, the top five primes received 30 percent of obligations in 2024, while the SVDG top 100 startups combined secured only $4.3 billion in awards in 2025.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Startups capture under 1% of contract obligations despite $118B raised; primes still dominate cash flows.
insights.quote: Silicon Valley Defense Group’s analysis shows that their top one hundred startups combined secured $4.3 billion in awards in 2025.
insights.locator: The Defense Department obligates over $450 billion

insights.claim: Government auditors found only 14 percent of 450 Defense Innovation Unit prototype OTA awards from 2016 to 2023 converted to production, rising to 51 percent among completed prototypes.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Base-rate conversion is low; prototype wins should not be modeled as production revenue.
insights.quote: only 14 percent converted from prototype to production (although the number rises to 51 percent among completed prototypes)
insights.locator: Government auditors reviewed 450 Defense Innovation Unit

insights.claim: The Pentagon reported only $2 billion of production other transactions across the department in 2024 and does not track conversion of prototype OTAs into standard contracts.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Lack of conversion data makes the pipeline opaque for investors.
insights.quote: The Pentagon reported only $2 billion of production other transactions across the department in 2024

themes.theme: Production winners and their valuation risk

insights.claim: Only a few new entrants have reached production at venture scale, including Palantir's Maven and Army enterprise agreements, Anduril's Army contract and Collaborative Combat Aircraft, Saronic's Corsair, and Hawkeye 360's internationally diversified contracts.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: The investable production cohort is narrow and concentrated.

insights.claim: Anduril is valued at roughly 30 times revenue and Palantir has traded even higher, so growth-priced expectations can easily be derailed by Defense Department program delays.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Program slippage is a key multiple-compression risk for high-flying defense names.
insights.quote: Anduril is valued at roughly 30 times revenue, Palantir has traded even higher.
insights.locator: And in this new defense tech

insights.claim: Even production-stage startups face risks including non-guaranteed renewals, budget pressure, traditional competitors lobbying Congress, and uncertain politics after the midterms and into the next administration.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Programs of record are not risk-free; political cycle is a real overhang.

insights.claim: Production-market defense startups face lumpy revenue misses from program delays that can cause liquidity crunches, category-wide concerns from tech failures that primes don't suffer, and multiple compression that makes raises hard even as bookings grow.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Watch for down rounds and structured financings at production-stage names despite growing bookings.
insights.quote: multiple compressions could mean challenging raises even if bookings are growing

insights.claim: Recent defense-tech investment has concentrated in a smaller group of capital-intensive production companies such as Hadrian, Apex and Neros, whose true financial success is hard to determine and whose growth investors are less forgiving than early-stage ones.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Concentration of late-stage capital raises the stakes of any high-profile stumble.

insights.claim: Exit paths for production startups are unclear because current valuations make acquisitions by traditional primes extremely difficult and the IPO market for defense specialists lacks visibility on future revenue and earnings.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Liquidity for defense-tech LPs is constrained; expect longer holds or discounted exits.
insights.quote: The biggest question for startups in production is how to generate meaningful returns for investors.

insights.claim: Hawkeye 360's recent listing was oversubscribed and opened successfully but the stock has declined since despite strong business execution.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Public markets may not reward defense-tech IPOs at private-market prices, a caution for the listing pipeline.
insights.quote: Hawkeye 360’s recent listing was oversubscribed and successful at opening, but the stock has declined since despite strong business execution.

themes.theme: Venture fund lifecycle as the key driver

insights.claim: Because the Pentagon's sluggishness is a constant, investor behavior rather than startup behavior is now the best predictor of growth, churn or downturn in defense tech.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Track fund closes, round terms and LP sentiment as the primary sector signal.
insights.quote: the behavior of investors is a better predictor for increased growth, churn, or a marked downturn

insights.claim: Venture funds that fueled early-2020s defense raises have fully deployed capital and face LP demands for cash exits, so they will lack patience or capital to keep funding illiquid portfolio companies, and growth investors will not provide runway absent production contracts.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Expect a funding gap for Series A/B defense startups and rising distress over the next few years.
insights.quote: They will not have the patience or capital to keep funding portfolio companies short on liquidity

insights.claim: Generalist VC firms that entered defense on trend are discovering defense procurement does not scale like consumer software and lacks clear exit paths, while specialist defense investors near fund end and the limits of their patience.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Generalist capital is likely to retreat first, hitting trend-driven categories.
insights.quote: defense procurement does not scale like consumer software and does not offer clear exit paths

insights.claim: No single event will trigger a defense-tech downturn; simply continuing current conditions will let the math of fund lifecycles do the rest over time.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Downturn will be gradual and quiet, not a visible crash, so don't wait for a headline catalyst.
insights.quote: All that is required is for current conditions to continue, and math will do the rest over time.

insights.claim: Early-stage defense tech is already showing signs of capital flight, evidenced by slowing seed and Series A deals.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Early-stage deal velocity is a live indicator of sector stress.
insights.quote: The early-stage market is also at greater risk of capital flight, as evidenced by slowing seed and Series A deals.

insights.claim: Prototype-market exposure concentrates in startups dependent on a single internal champion, in oversupplied categories like attritable drones, counter-drone and generic AI, in generalist-backed firms, and in pure-play software that doesn't own workflows.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: A screening checklist for which defense startups are most likely to fail.
insights.quote: think attritable drones, counter-drone or generic AI

insights.claim: Upcoming stressors including another continuing resolution, midterm-driven congressional changes, operational tempo draining discretionary dollars, or a change of administration could worsen conditions or trigger capital flight in both markets.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Political calendar events are catalysts for further defense-tech funding stress.
insights.locator: Both markets will feel further pressure

themes.theme: Demand pockets in munitions and interceptors

insights.claim: Dwindling interceptor and long-range munition stockpiles, which traditional approaches will take too long to replenish, are creating opportunities for startups like Castelion and Covenant that already have initial contracts and real capital.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Munitions and interceptor replenishment is a bright spot for early-stage defense capital, contingent on conversion to programmed dollars.
insights.quote: Interceptors and long-range munition stockpiles are dwindling, traditional approaches will take too long to replenish

themes.theme: Failure modes, winners and losers, and M&A

insights.claim: Prototype-dependent companies will quietly run out of money with no single failure making news, so the prototype market's collapse can only be recognized after it has occurred, while production-startup failures will be more visible and a few high-profile collapses could deter investors.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Absence of bad news is not evidence of health in early-stage defense tech.
insights.quote: the fall of the prototype market can only be truly recognized after it has occurred

insights.claim: Assessing defense-tech health requires watching what does not happen: funds that fail to close, financings done with debt or restrictive terms, companies going silent, and contracts not awarded; aggregate production awards are the best leading indicator, while policy and budget announcements are the least helpful.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Build monitoring around production award data and financing terms, ignoring policy rhetoric.
insights.quote: The least helpful thing to watch is policy and budget announcements from either the executive or legislative branches.

insights.claim: Winners and losers fall into four categories: the Deserved Few leaders, Deserved Losers with generic tech or inexperienced teams, Undeserved Losers with real tech that run out of cash before contracts arrive or collapse under prior valuations and liquidity preferences, and Opportunistic Acquirers.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Useful taxonomy for portfolio triage and distressed-asset sourcing.

insights.claim: If primes and private equity platforms look beyond EBITDA-based valuation of production contracts, distressed startups with real contracts and differentiated tech but limited runway could become attractive acquisitions as valuations fall, with venture investors bearing the loss.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Primes and PE roll-ups could buy venture-funded capability at a discount; a potential tailwind for prime M&A.
insights.quote: venture investors would be the billpayer further undermining the argument to allocate future capital

insights.claim: Unprofitable defense startups should pursue exits alongside financing with at least six months of runway, while primes and PE should build disciplined roll-up strategies to buy distressed assets at the right price.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Signals a coming wave of defense-tech consolidation and discounted M&A.
insights.quote: a discounted landing beats insolvency that strands the team and technology

insights.claim: A viable production contract has a buyer with procurement dollars rather than an innovation-budget champion, a procurement line item in the appropriated budget, and a contract vehicle allowing awards without further competition.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Three-part test investors can apply to validate defense startup revenue quality.
insights.quote: contracts have a buyer with procurement dollars rather than a champion with an innovation budget

insights.claim: The only thing the Defense Department needs to do to secure the health of the defense-tech sector is award production contracts at scale; no further policy reforms or organizational changes are required.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Reform announcements are noise; contract volume is the variable that moves the sector.
insights.quote: all they need to do is award production contracts at scale
insights.locator: If the Defense Department and the services

insights.claim: Market turbulence is no reason to abandon defense tech, since the U.S. will still need venture-backed startups and disciplined operators who reach production can still deliver real returns to LPs.
insights.speaker: Ben FitzGerald
insights.so_what: Remain selectively long defense tech with focus on production pathways and capital discipline.
